summary: A 1970 note on interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network, by D. C. Walden. It discusses how programs on different computers might talk to each other. It was replaced by RFC 62.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 61 explores how programs on different computers could exchange messages. It uses numbered ports and matching SEND and RECEIVE operations, and was replaced by RFC 62.

subtitle: A 1970 proposal for matching messages between local and remote processes.

tldr.problem: Programs on separate computers needed a systematic way to communicate as part of a resource-sharing network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 61 models communication with processes, numbered ports, SEND and RECEIVE operations, and rendezvous sites that match remote requests.
tldr.outcome: This early note was replaced by RFC 62, according to the RFC metadata.

today: RFC 61 is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 62. It records an early proposal for interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network.

sections.title: Interprocess Communication
sections.content: RFC 61 considers a resource-sharing network in which autonomous computer systems can use one another's resources. It treats resource sharing as a problem of communication between processes and first proposes a model for a time-sharing system.
sections.plainLanguage: The note asks how programs on separate computers can communicate. It begins by describing how programs can exchange messages inside one computer.

sections.title: Ports, SEND, and RECEIVE
sections.content: In the model, a port is a numbered data path to or from a process. A process can place a SEND at one port, while another process makes a matching RECEIVE. The monitor matches the port numbers and transfers the message; the note also describes receiving from any process.
sections.plainLanguage: Processes use numbered ports to identify where messages go. A monitor matches a sender with a receiver and transfers the message.

sections.title: Matching Messages Across Sites
sections.content: For remote processes, the note adds a site to the SEND and RECEIVE operations. A rendezvous site keeps a table of unmatched requests and pairs a SEND with a RECEIVE. Once matched, the message is transmitted to the receiving site's process.
sections.plainLanguage: For communication between sites, a rendezvous site matches the sender's and receiver's requests. The sites identify ports and locations so the message can reach the intended process.
